inquiry.centralIdea: Groups often follow shared routines that keep every member safe.
inquiry.tuneIn: Why might animals stay close together in a group instead of going off alone?
inquiry.reflect: Communicators work well with others by sharing information and listening. How does staying close to a group help keep everyone safe?

passage.title: Pip the Little Penguin
passage.text:
Pip belonged to the smallest species of penguin in the world, and lived along the southern coast of Australia. Each morning, he swam out with dozens of others to hunt, diving for small fish using wings shaped more like flippers than feathers built for flight.

Penguins can't fly, but flippers make them fast, precise swimmers — ideal for chasing fish underwater rather than soaring above the waves.

At dusk, the penguins gathered offshore in a group before coming in together, rather than one at a time. Moving as a crowd made it harder for predators to target any single penguin — a system scientists call the ‘penguin parade’.

Pip waddled up the beach in the middle of the group, counting the shapes of his colony-mates ahead of him: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. His burrow, shared with his mother, waited just past the dunes.
